1.pericope_label: The former treatise have I made, O Theophilus, of all that Jesus began both to do and teach, Until the day in which he was taken up, after that he through the Holy Ghost had given commandments unto the apostles whom he had chosen: To whom also he shewed himself alive after his passion by many infallible proofs, being seen of them forty days, and speaking of the things pertaining to the kingdom of God: And, being assembled together with them, commanded them that they should not depart from Jerusalem, but wait for the promise of the Father, which, saith he, ye have heard of me. For John truly baptized with water; but ye shall be baptized with the Holy Ghost not many days hence.

schools.summary: Settle the title before the text, since the manuscripts vary from the bare word for acts, through acts of apostles, to acts of the holy apostles; the long form of the received text with its adjective is certainly wrong, and it is possible the book was given no title at all by its author. Note that the word means doings and not decrees, and that what is actually recorded is chiefly the work of two men, one commissioned to open the door to Jew and Gentile and the other sent to the heathen world. On the opening phrase, observe that the noun means a word or discourse and was used by Xenophon of the several books of a history, that the adjective is strictly first rather than former, and that a superlative used where only two are compared is a common idiom which allows but does not imply a third volume. Note also that the verb rendered began is characteristic of the earlier book, occurring there some thirty times, which is so far an indication of one author. On the dedication, allow the inference that dropping the honorific implies a more intimate friendship, but call it precarious. On the resurrection, remark that the Greek has no adjective answering to infallible, but that the noun was a technical term of the rhetoricians for proofs carrying certainty as against those merely probable, and that no other writer in these books uses it; that the word for being seen is peculiar and unusual, perhaps implying that the presence was not continuous but at intervals; and that this is the only passage which gives the length of the interval, forty days, with its counterpart in the forty days of the temptation. Finally, on the last gathering, deny that the participle can mean eating together, calling that etymology mistaken, and render it as assembling them; while granting that salt was the mark of hospitality and that he did on occasion eat with them.

Show how the two books are joined: the writer gathers up the sum of what he had handled before, that he may pass to what followed the ascension, and so defines the history of the gospel as a narration of what Christ did and said while he was conversant upon earth. Refuse the common gloss that the order of doing before teaching means there was first purity of life and then preaching; true though it is that a teacher should speak first with his life and then with his tongue, or he differs nothing from a stage-player, that is not the point here, which looks back rather to the description of a prophet mighty in deed and word. Make the ascension the end of the history, since our redemption was fully complete and finished then, and take the words he was taken up as meaning that he truly departed out of this world, against the dotings of those who imagine that in his ascension there was no alteration of place. Add that he did not so depart as to leave off caring for us, since in ordaining a perpetual government in his Church he declared his care to provide for our salvation. Then say why the resurrection is insisted on: without it the gospel loses its whole authority and falls flat to the ground, and no faith remains, for everything depends on our knowing and being persuaded that Christ, being alive, speaks to us from the heavens. Note the word used for the proofs, which Aristotle applies to what is necessary in signs, and prefer to render it proofs rather than arguments, since these were evident tokens serving instead of necessary demonstration. Observe finally that the apostles had done the work of apostles before, but only as criers stirring up their nation to hear their Master, and that their ordinary function was not laid upon them until after the resurrection.

Begin with the book itself, its place among the historical writings, and the variety of its names: the transactions of the apostles in one codex, the acts of the holy apostles in another, a fifth Gospel to some, the Gospel of the Holy Spirit to one writer and the demonstration of the resurrection to another, both of the last two being peculiarly descriptive of its contents, since all the promises of the gifts and graces of the Spirit are here shown fulfilled. Then mark the division of labour between the volumes, the first describing the acts of Jesus Christ and the second the acts of the Holy Ghost by the apostles. On the commandments given, take it that Christ communicated the Spirit to the disciples after his resurrection as he had not before, opening their understanding and breathing on them, so that from this time a measure of that light and power was constantly resident in them, enabling them to discern the meaning of the older Scriptures and to appoint what rites were needful. Enumerate the proofs of the resurrection and count them: the appearances to different persons at different times, the eating and drinking, the meeting kept by appointment in Galilee, the offering of the body to be touched and handled, the instruction in the doctrines of the kingdom, the showing to more than five hundred at once, and the continuance of these manifestations for forty days; and add the list of the several appearances as they have been enumerated. On the baptism, distinguish the two: the one was water and a sign of penitence in reference to the remission of sin, the other is of the Holy Ghost, for the destruction of sin, the illumination of the mind and the consolation of the heart. And draw from the promise a lesson about the word, that baptism does not always mean being plunged or immersed, since this promise was fulfilled by an outpouring.

Begin by lamenting how little the book is known, since to many persons it and its author are so unfamiliar that they are not even aware such a book exists; and take that as the reason for expounding it, so that a treasure of this kind may not remain hidden out of sight. Urge that it may profit us no less than the Gospels, being so replete with Christian wisdom and sound doctrine, especially in what is said concerning the Holy Ghost; and therefore that we should not hastily pass it by but examine it closely. Give the ground of the claim: the predictions which Christ utters in the Gospels may here be seen actually coming to pass, so that in the very facts the bright evidence of truth shines out, together with the mighty change taking place in the disciples now that the Spirit has come upon them. Instance the promise that whoever believes shall do the works that he did and greater, and the foretelling that they should be brought before rulers and kings and scourged in the synagogues and suffer grievous things and overcome all. Then on the baptism promised, press the completeness of it: the grace was not in part but in full perfection, for as the man who plunges into the water is encompassed on all sides by it, so were they baptized completely by the Spirit. Draw the distinction that gives the comparison its point, that the water flows round the outside only while the Spirit baptizes the soul within, and that completely; and take an example from matter, poor and common but useful for simpler folk, that when fire passes through the mass of the iron it makes the whole of it fire, so that what was cold becomes burning and what was black is made bright.

Put the reader in mind of the former book before entering on this one, so that he may see not only how this begins where that breaks off, but how, as in water face answers to face, the acts of the apostles answer to the acts of their Master, the acts of his grace. Then attend to the dedication. The man addressed was called most excellent in the earlier inscription and is here called only Theophilus, which need not mean that his excellency was diminished: perhaps he had quitted the place for the sake of which the title was given him; perhaps he had grown into years and despised such marks of respect more than he once did; perhaps the writer was now more intimate with him and could address him with the more freedom. Note that it was usual with the ancients, Christian and heathen writers alike, to inscribe their books to some particular person, and that the directing of a book to one man does not narrow its use to him.

debates.question: What is the book's proper title?

sides.position: The manuscripts vary from the bare word for acts upward; the received long form with holy is certainly wrong, and the book may have had no title at all
It has borne many names — transactions of the apostles, a fifth Gospel, the Gospel of the Holy Spirit, the demonstration of the resurrection
The word means doings and not decrees, and what is recorded is chiefly the work of two men

debates.question: Why is the dedication shorter than the Gospel's?

sides.position: Perhaps he had quitted the office the title belonged to, or grown old enough to despise such forms, or the writer was now more intimate with him
The inference is allowable but precarious

debates.question: Does the participle at verse four mean assembling or eating together?

sides.position: Assembling: the Greek has not the other sense, and the etymology behind it is mistaken
It is derived not from salt but from the noun for an assembly
Several good manuscripts read the word for living or eating together
Salt was the mark of hospitality, and he did on occasion eat with them, but the other sense is doubtful

outliers.note: Alone begins by complaining that the book is so little known that many are unaware it exists, and argues that it may profit us no less than the Gospels because in it the predictions uttered there are seen coming to pass.

Alone turns the forty days against a rabbinic slander that used the same number, observing that the man so accused gave the sufficient testimony to his own innocence by conversing among men for forty days after death.

6.pericope_label: When they therefore were come together, they asked of him, saying, Lord, wilt thou at this time restore again the kingdom to Israel? And he said unto them, It is not for you to know the times or the seasons, which the Father hath put in his own power. But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.

schools.summary: Note the resumptive particle, which links what follows to the introductory verses and marks the beginning of the narrative proper, and the imperfect of the verb, which shows they asked repeatedly before he answered. Explain what was still wrong with the expectation: before the passion they had thought the kingdom of God should immediately appear, those hopes had seemed to fail, and the resurrection had revived them, but they were still predominantly national, so that even the Twelve were thinking not of a kingdom embracing all mankind but of a sovereignty restored to Israel. Fix the scene at the Mount of Olives — or place it, with others, on a mountain of Galilee. Then take the two words for time: one denotes periods and the other points, though the distinction is not always maintained, and the pair is characteristic of this writer and of Paul. Observe that the answer touches the season rather than the nature of the fulfilment, leaving them to the teaching of the Spirit and of time to remould their expectations, and that what was needed now was the patience which waits for that teaching. Remark how eager people have always been to fix definite dates for the second coming, just as the apostles were about the political kingdom, and take the reservation of these things to the Father's own authority as a gentle hint about the limits of curiosity. Then object to the English, which renders two different Greek words by the same noun: the first is authority, the second is the energy communicated. Insist that the power promised is not the power they had in view, with its organisation and equipment on the Roman model, and that their very question proved their need of the other kind. Finally, find the plan of the whole book in the last clause, since Jerusalem, Judaea, Samaria and the uttermost part of the earth answer to its great divisions, and note that the word for witnesses is the one from which our martyrs comes.

Observe first that they were gathered together when the question was moved, so that it came not from the foolishness of one or two but by the common consent of them all; and then say plainly how bad the question was. It is marvellous rudeness that men diligently instructed for three whole years should betray no less ignorance than if they had never heard a word, and there are as many errors in the question as there are words in it. They ask about a kingdom, but dream of an earthly one flowing with riches and dainties and outward peace; they assign the present time to its restoring, desiring to triumph before the battle and to have their wages before they begin to work; and they restrain the kingdom of Christ to the carnal Israel, which was rather to be spread abroad. Then take the answer as a general reprehension of the whole question, since it was too curious of them to desire to know what their Master would have them ignorant of; and lay down the rule of learning from it, that we should go as far forward as our Master goes in teaching, and be willing to be ignorant of what he conceals, since there is naturally engendered in us a foolish curiosity and a rash boldness which this admonition corrects. On what follows, note that Christ calls them back to the promise and to the commandment together, which was the readiest way to bridle their curiosity, since curiosity rises almost always either of idleness or of distrust, distrust being cured by meditating on the promises and idleness by attending to our duty. Charge them accordingly with catching preposterously at gifts proper to the Spirit before they were endued with him, and with wishing, when they had been called out to warfare, to omit their labour and take their ease in the inn. Add what the correction implies, that instead of the worldly ease and riches they were looking for they must expect labour, service, afflictions and trials, which would require the very power promised.

Place the meeting on one of the mountains of Galilee, and state the expectation plainly: the disciples, in common with the Jews, looked for a kingdom at least in part secular, and continued in that opinion more or less until the day of Pentecost, when the outpouring of the Spirit taught them its spiritual nature. The kingdom had for a considerable time been taken away from Israel and the Romans held the government, so the object of the question seems to have been to learn from their all-knowing Master whether the time was now fully come for the Romans to be thrust out. Note also that they came in a body, having concerted the design beforehand, and that they still seemed to dream of an outward kingdom in which the Jews should have dominion over all nations. On the two words for time, take the first for any large portion of a period, an era, an olympiad, a lustrum or a year, and the second for the particular part or opportunity within it in which it might be proper to do a work; and draw the doctrine out. God has fixed the great periods in which he will bring about those revolutions his wisdom and justice have designed, but leaves himself at liberty to choose the particular portions of them; so that God is no necessary agent, everything being under his own control and authority, and he will not form decrees of which he must then become the necessary executor, the infinite liberty of acting or not acting being essential to him. Then distinguish the two Greek words rendered power, since translating different terms by the same English word is a source of error: the one marks God's authority over times and seasons and his uncompellable liberty, the other the energy communicated to the disciples by which they were enabled to work miracles, the word being sometimes put for the miracle itself. Conclude that they were to be empowered to witness the gospel both by their preaching and by their suffering.

Explain the manner of the asking before the matter of it. When the disciples intend to ask anything they approach him together, that by dint of numbers they may abash him into compliance. They knew well enough that in saying of that day knoweth no man he had merely declined to tell them, and therefore they drew near and put the question again; they would not have put it had they been truly satisfied with that answer. Give two reasons why they asked now: having heard that they were about to receive the Holy Ghost, they thought themselves worthy of instruction and desired to learn; and they were quite ready for freedom, having no mind to address themselves to danger, and wishing only to breathe freely again, since no light matters had happened to them but the utmost peril had impended over them. Note also what they left out and what they pressed, that they said nothing to him of the Holy Ghost, and that they did not ask when, but whether at this time. Then take the answer as the correction of curiosity, and let the warning cut both ways: as to the time let no one be curious, and venture not to declare when these things shall be; but on the other hand do not supinely slumber, for the word is watch, since in such an hour as you expect not the Son of Man comes. Add why some knowledge of the signs was needful, that we should not die deceived nor be led astray by the false one; and observe that it was by a providential arrangement that the apostles addressed themselves on this matter to the True Teacher.

Notice how the meeting came about, since he had appointed them to Galilee and then appointed them to Jerusalem again, and so tried their obedience, which was found ready and cheerful; they came together as he appointed, to be the witnesses of his ascension. Then observe the question they asked at this interview. They came to him as those who had consulted one another about it and concurred in it unanimously; they came in a body and put it as the sense of the house. Allow that the question may be taken two ways, and set out the more favourable of them: it may carry a repudiation of the present rulers of Israel, the chief priests and elders who had put him to death and had tamely given up the kingdom to Caesar and owned themselves his subjects, so that the disciples are asking whether such men shall continue to hold what they have so ill used.

debates.question: Why did they put the question together?

sides.position: So that by dint of numbers they might abash him into compliance, not being satisfied with his earlier refusal
They came in a body and put it as the sense of the house
The design was concerted beforehand
It came by the common consent of them all, and there are as many errors in it as words

debates.question: How firm is the distinction between the two words for time?

sides.position: One is any large stretch, an era or a year; the other the particular opportunity within it
A longer and a shorter space
One indefinite, the other fixed
Sometimes periods and points, but the distinction is not always maintained

debates.question: Where did the scene take place?

sides.position: At the Mount of Olives
On one of the mountains of Galilee

outliers.note: Alone turns the reservation of times and seasons into an argument about the divine nature, that God is no necessary agent and frames no decree of which he must then become the compelled executor.
Alone turns the verse on the reader, remarking how eager people have always been to fix dates for the second coming, exactly as the apostles were about their political kingdom.

9.pericope_label: And when he had spoken these things, while they beheld, he was taken up; and a cloud received him out of their sight. And while they looked stedfastly toward heaven as he went up, behold, two men stood by them in white apparel; Which also said, Ye men of Galilee, why stand ye gazing up into heaven? this same Jesus, which is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go into heaven.

schools.summary: Say why the manner of the departure mattered and was recorded so exactly. It is not affirmed anywhere that they saw him rise from the dead, because the evidence of that could be better established by seeing him afterwards; but the ascension could not be confirmed in that way, and so it was arranged that he should go in open day, in their presence, and not while they were asleep or indifferent but while they were engaged in conversation and looking at him. Had he vanished secretly, or by night, they would have been amazed and confounded, and might have doubted whether they were not deceived. Note the participles: they were looking directly at him, he was lifted up, and the cloud took him under, so that he seemed to be supported by it as it bore him from their eyes; and note that several different verbs are used elsewhere of the same event. Then raise the difficulty about the silence of the Gospels, since it is remarkable how little stress is laid there on a fact always so prominent in the creeds, two of the four not recording it at all and a third mentioning it with the utmost brevity. Answer it thus: it was because the Ascension was from the first part of the creed of Christendom that the Evangelists said so little; the fact had been taught to every catechumen, and they would not embellish it with fantastic details as later legends embellished other things. Describe the gazing as the intense look of those deeply interested, mingled here of amazement, disappointment and curiosity, together with the desire to catch the last glimpse of a beloved Master. On the two figures, prefer were standing, the appearance being sudden and the approach unnoticed, and compare them with those seen at the empty sepulchre, bright and clad in white like the young priests of the Temple. Finally, on the promised return, note that the personal name is itself the assurance, and that the emphatic doubling of the phrase covers the manner of the coming as well as the fact of it.

Take the ascension as one of the chief points of our faith, and show how carefully its certainty was confirmed. If he had vanished away secretly the disciples might have stood astonished, doubting what had become of him; but as it was, they were standing on an elevated spot, open on all sides, with nothing to interrupt the view, and they saw taken up the very man with whom they had been conversant, whom they had just heard speak and were beholding with their eyes. On the two who appeared, decline to argue whether they had real bodies, saying only that certain it is they were not men, since Scripture commonly speaks so; and take their garments as a token of rare and excellent dignity, given that God might distinguish them by an evident mark from the common sort, so that the disciples should give the better ear to them and we at this day should know the vision was shown of God. Then defend the disciples against the appearance of a rebuke. Do not think the name given them was opprobrious, as though the angels meant to reprehend their dullness; it was rather to make them attentive, that men whom they had never seen before should name them as though they knew them perfectly. And meet the objection that they seem reprehended without cause for looking up into heaven, since where should they rather seek for Christ than there, and does not Scripture often exhort us to it? Answer that they were not reproved for looking heavenward, but first because they coveted to see Christ with their bodily senses when the cloud had been put between, and secondly because they hoped he would return again straightway, whereas he had ascended to remain in the heavens until the appointed time.

Describe the going up exactly, that he was speaking face to face with them and while they beheld was taken up, and that they continued to look after him until a cloud received him out of their sight, that is, until he had ascended above the region of the clouds, by whose density all further distinct vision was prevented. Say that these circumstances are very remarkable and should be carefully noted, because they make a certain theory insupportable — the theory that our Lord did not ascend to heaven at all, that his being taken up means his going into some mountain whose top was covered with clouds or thick vapours, and that the two men in white were two priests or Levites informing the disciples that he would visit them again at some future time. Add that one would suppose such an opinion could hardly obtain credit among people professing Christianity, and yet it is espoused by some men of considerable learning and ingenuity; and press the same point again at the next verse, that the gazing was not toward the top of a mountain, to which an unbridled fancy influenced by infidelity would have him ascend, but toward heaven. Take the two men for angels in human shape, and their white apparel as emblematical of their purity, happiness and glory. On the promise of the return, say it is the same Jesus, clothed in human nature, who shall come with the same body, descending from heaven by his own sovereign and all-controlling power, to judge the quick and the dead; and report the very ancient opinion among Christians that he will make his appearance on the Mount of Olives, noting also that some refer the angels' words instead to his coming to destroy the Jewish nation.

Look back over the interval before going forward. Since the blessed and glorious Resurrection, whereby the divine power in three days raised the true Temple of God which the wickedness of men had overthrown, the sacred forty days are now ended, which by most holy appointment were devoted to our most profitable instruction; for during the period that the Lord thus protracted the lingering of his bodily presence, our faith in the Resurrection was fortified by needful proofs. Give the reason those proofs were needed, and give it without flattering the apostles: Christ's death had much disturbed the disciples' hearts, and a kind of torpor of distrust had crept over their grief-laden minds at his torture on the cross, at his giving up the ghost, at the burial of his lifeless body. Instance what followed, that when the holy women brought word of the stone rolled away, of the sepulchre emptied of the body, and of the angels bearing witness to a living Lord, their words seemed like ravings to the Apostles and the other disciples. Let that doubtfulness be the measure of what the forty days were for, and of why the departure at the end of them was made so plain.

debates.question: Why do the Gospels say so little about the Ascension?

sides.position: Because it was from the first part of the creed, taught to every catechumen, so the Evangelists had no motive to embellish it
The manner was recorded exactly because the fact could not be established as the resurrection was, by later appearances
Its certainty was confirmed by the circumstances — an open place, full view, and the man they had just heard speak
Angels in human shape, the white apparel emblematic of purity and glory
Certainly not men, whatever their bodies; the garments a token of dignity, that the disciples should give the better ear
Forms like those at the empty sepulchre, clad like the young priests of the Temple

debates.question: Is there a rebuke in the address to the men of Galilee?

sides.position: No reproach in the name, but a slight censure in the question
Not opprobrious at all, but meant to fix their attention, since strangers named them as if they knew them
Not aimed at their country, but showing the speakers knew them and marking the grace that chose such mean persons

outliers.note: Alone raises the difficulty that the Gospels say so little of an event so prominent in the creeds, and answers it by the very fact that it was creed already and needed no embellishing.

Alone accounts for the forty days by the disciples' state after the crucifixion, when a torpor of distrust had crept over their grief-laden minds and the women's report of the empty tomb seemed to them like raving.

12.pericope_label: Then returned they unto Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet, which is from Jerusalem a sabbath day's journey. And when they were come in, they went up into an upper room, where abode both Peter, and James, and John, and Andrew, Philip, and Thomas, Bartholomew, and Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus, and Simon Zelotes, and Judas the brother of James. These all continued with one accord in prayer and supplication, with the women, and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brethren.

schools.summary: Give the rule behind the phrase about the sabbath day's journey: it is as far as a Jew might lawfully travel on that day, two thousand paces or cubits, seven furlongs and a half, not quite a mile — a limit not determined by the law of Moses but fixed by the teachers, who reasoned from the command that no one should go out of his place, some reckoning the bounds by the compass of the Israelites' camp before the scribes settled on two thousand cubits, the suburbs of the city. Then be careful what is inferred from it. The text says only that the mount is that distance from the city, not that Jesus was precisely so far off when he ascended; the Gospel places the scene over against Bethany, some fifteen furlongs, while the top of the mount is six. Note, too, that the mention of the distance and the measure chosen are both remarkable, and may suggest a reckoning in which the forty days had already expired and this last meeting fell on the following sabbath, eight days before Pentecost — with a certain fitness in the Lord entering his rest on the great day of rest. On the room, mark the article and the word: it is the upper room, the loft under the flat roof used for retirement and prayer, to be distinguished from the guest-chamber on the floor below where meals were taken and the Passover eaten; and hold that it was in a private house rather than in the temple, the statement that they were continually in the temple meaning on proper occasions. Take the adverb of one accord as with the same mind or spirit, note the periphrastic imperfect of a verb meaning to stick at a thing, and observe that they kept at the praying until the answer came. On the women, think of them as among the writer's own informants, since he alone of the Evangelists names them as a body, and note that here we lose sight of them and all that follows is conjecture.

Take the return and the lodging together. They dwelt in one upper parlour, which was the part of a house usually let out to tenants, the more commodious rooms being reserved by the owners for themselves; so the word signifies that they were confined to a narrow space, and yet, though this inconvenience was great, they did not part asunder. They might have been more comfortably separate, but they were not to break company before the Spirit came; and the noting of the distance lends credit to the history. On the list of names, refuse two conclusions commonly drawn from it. That Peter is reckoned first does not prove his supremacy: grant that he was the chief of the apostles, and it still does not follow that he was chief ruler of all the world; and if precedence in a catalogue settles rank, then the mother of Christ must be inferior to all the other women, since she is reckoned last of them. Then on the word rendered women, prefer wives: the word may be interpreted either way, but since the apostles afterwards carried their wives about with them, as Paul testifies, it is not likely they were then apart, for they might more easily rest together in one place than change their abode by wandering to and fro; and since they were looking for the coming of the Holy Ghost, then even at hand, what reason was there why they should deprive their wives of it? Add finally what the whole picture is for, that they continued together in prayer, waiting for what had been promised.

State the measure first: the Jews generally fix a sabbath day's journey at two thousand cubits, which is not a mile. Then meet the geographical difficulty, since the mount was but five furlongs from the city while Bethany was fifteen: the first tract of the mount, called Bethany, lay a sabbath day's journey from the city, and the tract called Bethphage extended the same distance, so that when our Lord came to the place where the two tracts touched each other, he there ascended, which place was distant from Jerusalem exactly a sabbath day's journey. On the upper room, allow that it may have been a room in the temple or in the house of one of the disciples, and incline to the temple, since it is said that after their return they were continually in the temple praising and blessing God; but grant that upper rooms in private houses were used for reading the law and conferring on religious matters, and note that this room seems to have been where all the apostles lodged. Take such chambers generally as rooms in the highest part of a house, set apart by the Jews for private prayer, which the apostles now used for all the offices of religion. On the last verse, report that many manuscripts and versions omit the words for supplication and that Griesbach struck them out; but refuse the argument that the two words mean the same thing, for prayer may imply any address to God in the way of petition, while supplication is the earnest, affectionate and continued application for the blessing requested: prayer asks, supplication expostulates, entreats, urges and re-urges the petition. Add that the brethren named at the close were near kinsmen who for some time did not believe, it seems not until near his death.

Draw an inference from the measure that no one else draws. It seems that it was also on a sabbath-day that these things took place; for the writer would not thus have specified the distance, saying from the mount called Olivet, which is from Jerusalem a sabbath day's journey, unless they were then going on the sabbath-day a certain definite distance. Note also why they were able to return at all: they could not have borne it if the angel had not referred them to another Coming. Then follow the narrative closely as it proceeds. When they were come in they went up into an upper room where they were making their abode, so that they remained in Jerusalem after the Resurrection; and observe the order of the names, that it is no longer only the one brother mentioned together with the other, but Peter and the two together, and after them the rest.

Say whence he ascended and why the place was fitting. It was from the Mount of Olives, from that part of it where the town of Bethany stood; there he had begun his sufferings, and therefore there he rolled away the reproach of them by his glorious ascension, so showing that his passion and his ascension had the same reference and tendency. Thus would he enter upon his kingdom in the sight of Jerusalem, and of those undutiful and ungrateful citizens of his who would not have him reign over them. Note that it was prophesied of him that his feet should stand upon the Mount of Olives, which is before Jerusalem, and that presently after it is added that the Mount of Olives shall cleave in two; so that from the mount of Olives he ascended who is himself the olive tree.

debates.question: What follows from the sabbath day's journey being mentioned?

sides.position: That the day was itself a sabbath, or the distance would not have been given that way
That the forty days had expired and this meeting fell on the following sabbath, eight days before Pentecost
Nothing about where Jesus stood: the text says only that the mount is that far from the city
The apparent discrepancy is solved where the tracts of Bethany and Bethphage touch

debates.question: Was the upper room in the temple or in a private house?

sides.position: Not a private house at all but the temple
Probably the temple, since they were continually there, though private upper rooms were also so used
There is no evidence for the temple and it is not very probable
A private house; continually means on proper occasions
Nearly synonymous
Not so: prayer asks, supplication expostulates, entreats and urges the petition again
They stuck to the praying until the answer came

outliers.note: Alone infers the day of the week from the measure of the distance, reasoning that it would not have been stated as a sabbath day's journey unless they were then walking such a distance on the sabbath.

Alone uses the list of names against two conclusions at once, denying that Peter's standing first proves supremacy on the ground that the same reasoning would make the mother of Christ inferior to all the women, since she is named last.

15.pericope_label: And in those days Peter stood up in the midst of the disciples, and said, (the number of names together were about an hundred and twenty,) Men and brethren, this scripture must needs have been fulfilled, which the Holy Ghost by the mouth of David spake before concerning Judas, which was guide to them that took Jesus. For he was numbered with us, and had obtained part of this ministry. Now this man purchased a field with the reward of iniquity; and falling headlong, he burst asunder in the midst, and all his bowels gushed out. And it was known unto all the dwellers at Jerusalem; insomuch as that field is called in their proper tongue, Aceldama, that is to say, The field of blood. For it is written in the book of Psalms, Let his habitation be desolate, and let no man dwell therein: and his bishoprick let another take.

schools.summary: Take the number first. The word for names is a Hebraism for persons, found so in the Greek of the older Scriptures and in the Revelation, and the phrase means they were gathered in the same place; a hundred and twenty is a crowd for such a room, and there is no special significance in the figure beyond its being how many were there. Or say the number probably included the Seventy, perhaps also Joseph of Arimathaea and Nicodemus and some of the five hundred who had seen their risen Lord, and that the use of names suggests a list from which the writer extracted the most conspicuous. Note the reading brethren for disciples, and that the form of address is more dignified and respectful than a bare brethren, women being included though the noun refers to men. On the speaker, hear the tone of one who felt his offence fully forgiven and himself restored to his former position as guide and leader, doing the work faithfully being a worthier fruit of repentance than any public confession would have been; and observe that the Spirit has not yet come upon him, so that the necessity he points out is a logical and not a moral one. Treat the account of the traitor's death as a long parenthesis by the historian, resumed at the citation. Note that the word rendered falling headlong means rather flat on the face as against on the back, and that the place suits the tradition of the hanging; and that two explanations of the field's name survive, the one deriving it from the price of blood and the other from the blood shed there, both of which may be true, since an ill-omened name can carry a double emphasis. On the citation, note that it follows neither the Hebrew nor the Greek exactly, the plural being made singular and a clause about tents omitted; and that the word rendered bishopric means over-seership, to visit and inspect, the ecclesiastical sense coming later.

Give the reason for filling the vacancy. It was meet that another should be chosen in the place of Judas, lest through the treachery of one man all that Christ had appointed should seem made of none effect; he did not unadvisedly choose twelve at the beginning as the principal preachers of his gospel, and when he said they should be judges of the twelve tribes he showed it was done of set purpose, that they might gather the tribes into one faith. So the number was as it were holy, and had it been left diminished by the wickedness of Judas the preaching would have suffered by it. Then refuse the inference drawn from Peter's speaking. Because Peter speaks in this assembly the Papists will have him head of the universal Church — as though no man might speak in any assembly of the godly but he must straightway be Pope. Grant that in every assembly some must be chief, and that the apostles ascribed this honour to Peter; but ask what that makes for their claim, and having bidden them adieu, consider rather what the Spirit speaks by Peter's mouth. Then treat the account of the death as an insertion by the historian and enclose it in a parenthesis, for four reasons: the disciples already knew it well enough; it would be absurd to tell men standing in Jerusalem that the field was so called by the inhabitants of Jerusalem; it would be stranger still to explain a word of their own mother tongue; and the answer that Peter was addressing Galileans of a different speech is vain and frivolous, since the difference was one of pronunciation only. Add why the scripture is cited at all, that no one's mind should be troubled by so horrible a fall in one chosen to so excellent a function.

Read brethren rather than disciples, since it was not merely among the disciples that he stood but among the whole company; and make something of the number, for a hundred and twenty was what the Jews required to form a council in any city, so that the disciples, gathering that number out of the many already converted, formed a complete council in whose presence the important business of the election could properly be transacted. Take the citation as a strong attestation to the inspiration of the Psalms, which were dictated by the Holy Spirit and spoken by the mouth of David. On the field, say that Judas probably did not purchase it himself, the money he was paid being so applied; though it is possible he had designed to buy a field and was in treaty for it, and the priests, knowing his intention, completed the purchase after his death and used the ground for the burial of strangers. Note that the repentance of Judas, his dying testimony to our Lord's innocence, his tragical death and the transaction about the field were all publicly known, that the name arose from them, and that these circumstances must have lessened the credit of the chief priests and prepared the public mind to receive the gospel afterwards; and that the proper tongue meant is not Hebrew, which had long ceased to be spoken in Palestine, but a sort of Chaldaeo-Syriac. Then object to the last word of the passage: to render it bishopric is not proper, since the office of Judas was widely different from what we call a bishopric, with its diocese, estate and emoluments; the Greek means simply an overseer or superintendent, from the words for over and to see, and our English word is a corruption of it through the Saxon. Say plainly that what is meant is his apostleship.

Show what the vacancy cost and why it had to be filled before the Spirit came. The sin of Judas was not only his own shame and ruin but made a gap in the college of the apostles. They were ordained twelve, with an eye to the twelve tribes of Israel descended from the twelve patriarchs; they were the twelve stars that make up the church's crown, and for them twelve thrones were designated. Now, being twelve while they were learners, if they were but eleven when they came to be teachers, it would set every one enquiring what had become of the twelfth, and so revive the remembrance of the scandal of their society. Therefore care was taken, before the descent of the Spirit, to fill up the vacancy; and it is likely that our Lord had given directions about it among the other things he spoke pertaining to the kingdom of God.

debates.question: Is the number a hundred and twenty significant?

sides.position: Yes: it was what the Jews required to constitute a council in a city, so a complete court was formed
No special significance; just the number there, and a crowd for the room
It probably included the Seventy and others, and the word names hints at a written list

debates.question: Is the account of Judas part of Peter's speech?

sides.position: No: four things forbid it, and it should be read in a parenthesis
No; and the reply that Peter spoke to Galileans of another speech is vain and frivolous
A parenthesis by the historian, resumed at the citation
He hanged himself and then fell and burst asunder
The rope seems to have broken at or just before death
The devil caught him into the air, strangled him and dashed him on the ground; the Greek need not mean he hanged himself
The word means flat on the face rather than headlong

outliers.note: Alone proposes that the devil caught Judas into the air as soon as the money was flung back, strangled him and dashed him on the ground, and questions whether the Greek need mean that he hanged himself at all.
Alone makes the hundred and twenty a deliberate figure, that being the quorum the Jews required for a council, so that a complete court was assembled for the election.

21.pericope_label: Wherefore of these men which have companied with us all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, Beginning from the baptism of John, unto that same day that he was taken up from us, must one be ordained to be a witness with us of his resurrection. And they appointed two, Joseph called Barsabas, who was surnamed Justus, and Matthias. And they prayed, and said, Thou, Lord, which knowest the hearts of all men, shew whether of these two thou hast chosen, That he may take part of this ministry and apostleship, from which Judas by transgression fell, that he might go to his own place. And they gave forth their lots; and the lot fell upon Matthias; and he was numbered with the eleven apostles.

schools.summary: State the qualification and its consequence. The Twelve must present themselves in their symbolic completeness, as sent to the twelve tribes, and the gap must be filled by one qualified to bear witness of what had been said and done during the ministry and above all of the resurrection, which even by Paul's reckoning was a condition of apostleship. Note that the one chosen must be a personal witness able to speak from his own experience of the ministry, resurrection and ascension — and note further what follows from that, that such a qualification will soon put an end to those who can bear such testimony. Explain the phrase about going in and out as a familiar idiom for the whole course of a life, and observe that the participle rendered beginning agrees with the Lord and marks his ministry as beginning with the baptism of John and lasting until the Ascension. On the two candidates, leave it uncertain whether the apostles presented them to the choice of the whole body or the community chose them for decision by lot, and record what is known of the first, that he must have been a disciple almost from the beginning, that his surname may have been a patronymic, and that he is said to have been one of the Seventy. On the prayer, note the compound word for heart-knower, found again only once in these books, and that the petition assumes the choice already made and asks only that it be shown. Raise the question whether the prayer is addressed to the Son, with a recollection of his insight into men's hearts, or to the Father, and set the two analogies against each other. On the last verse, hold that lots and not votes are meant, both from the prayer and from the word fell; describe the tablets placed in an urn and shaken until one came out; and note that to a Jew the lot suggested not gambling but the old method of learning the will of God.

Meet the objection that the citation proves too little. It might seem far-fetched that because David spoke of transferring the office of Judas, the disciples should therefore choose a successor; but they knew that the charge of ordering the Church was given them, and once Peter had told them it pleased the Lord that it should be so, he gathers that they ought to do it — for whenever God is pleased to use our agency in maintaining the government of his Church, we must not linger once we know his will, but stoutly perform what is required. Note also that the choice was to be of one of the men, and of one from among themselves, known to them, whose ability and integrity had been tried. Then ask why two were presented when only one was to be chosen. Was it that they were so alike that they could not discern which was fitter? That would have been no reason to leave it to a lot. Was Joseph the more esteemed? Or were they diversely affected? That is scarcely probable, and not to be admitted, given the excellent testimony just borne to their unity and agreement, and it would have been absurd to pollute the election of an apostle with such strife. On the office named, observe that the word ministry is a lowly one and apostleship is added for dignity, though the sense is plainest if the two are taken together as the ministry of the apostleship; the writer meant to join the excellency of the office to its burden, and to declare that the apostles are called to a painful function. Finally, defend the lot itself. Those who think it wickedness to cast lots at all offend partly through ignorance and partly because they do not understand the word; divination by lots is altogether devilish, but when magistrates divide provinces or brethren an inheritance it is lawful, Solomon making God the governor of the event.

Object first to the English. There is no term answering to ordained in the Greek at all, and the translation misleads every reader who cannot examine the original; an older printed version renders the two verses more faithfully and more clearly as one sentence without it. Say that the men judged it necessary to fill the vacancy with one who had been an eye-witness of our Lord's acts, and that the two put forward were probably of the number of the Seventy and so well fitted; it is likely the disciples were themselves divided which of the two to prefer, and therefore laid the matter before God that he might decide it by lot. Mark exactly where human counsel stops: so far the faithful could go by consulting together, but no further, and here commences the proper use of the lot, whereby a matter of importance which cannot be determined by any ordinary method is committed to the divine decision. On the prayer, take the compound title as an attribute of God, who knows the hearts, the most secret purposes and dispositions of all men, and who therefore knew which of the two he had best qualified by natural and gracious dispositions for the work. On the closing phrase about his own place, report that it has been variously expounded, and note the variants, one copy reading place for lot and another just for own, so that the sense would be that he might go to his just or proper place. Describe the casting of the lot in its simplest form, two pieces of metal or slips of parchment inscribed with the names put into an urn, and after prayer one drawn out; and trace the Greek verb for numbering him with the eleven to the word for the pebble which the ancients used both in voting and in reckoning.

debates.question: Why were two candidates put forward for one place?

sides.position: Not because they were indistinguishable, nor because one was more esteemed, nor from division, which the testimony to their unity forbids
It is uncertain whether the apostles presented them to the body or the body chose them for the lot
The disciples were divided which to prefer and so laid it before God
So far consultation could go and no further; there the proper use of the lot begins

debates.question: To whom is the prayer addressed?

sides.position: There are strong reasons for supposing it was made to the Lord Jesus
The analogy of a later prayer favours the Father, though prayer to the Son was not foreign to them
It assumes God has already chosen and asks only that the choice be shown

debates.question: Whose is the own place spoken of?

sides.position: Judas's: the rabbis use the phrase of hell, as of Balaam and of the friends of Job
Judas's: he made ready his own berth and went to it
Most naturally Judas's, though the grammar allows it of the man about to be chosen taking his place among the Twelve
A variant would read his just or proper place

outliers.note: Alone draws out the consequence of the qualification demanded, that a requirement of personal eyewitness must very soon exhaust the supply of men able to meet it.
Alone defends the casting of lots against those who condemn the practice outright, distinguishing devilish divination from the lawful dividing of provinces or of an inheritance.
